newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU expected to agree food irradiation compromise.
newsitem.headline: EU expected to agree food irradiation compromise.

text.p: The European Union is expected next week to agree a compromise solution on the sensitive issue of treating foodstuffs with ionizing radiation to increase their shelf life and to remove pests, EU diplomats said on Friday.

The Dutch EU presidency hopes the bloc's internal market ministers will reach a political agreement on Wednesday on the proposal, first put forward in 1988 as part of the bloc's bid to create a single market.
Food irradiation is a physical method of processing food like heat treatment, freezing or additives.
EU diplomats said the compromise proposal seeks to strike a balance between those countries wanting free trade in all irradiated foodstuffs now and those which want to limit it.
Germany, Denmark, Sweden and Austria are generally seen as being suspicious of this way of treating food.

Under the plan, the EU would agree on two sets of legislation, one which would lay down general provisions and another which would establish an initial positive list of foodstuffs which can be treated with ionizing radiation.

The EU executive would by the end of 2002 propose a final list of foodstuffs which may be irradiated. EU countries would be able to keep national bans on all foodstuffs or food ingredients not included on the list.

The initial list would be limited to dried aromatic herbs, spices and vegetable seasonings. Such products are often contaminated or infested with organisms harmful to human health. The idea is to increase the number of products gradually.
In addition, all ingredients treated with ionizing radiation must be mentioned on the labelling of foodstuffs.
Food irradiation would be allowed only if there is a reasonable technological need to do it, if it is beneficial for consumers and if there is no health hazard.
